title: BEAMOS revival: electron-beam addressed storage with no access transistor
idea: Revive GE's 1970s BEAMOS: a MEMS-deflected array of molybdenum field-emitter microcolumns (one per ~64k-bit tile, in a vacuum cavity wafer-bonded over the die) writes and reads charge on fully floating MOS storage islands via secondary-emission balance, so no bit is ever tied to a transistor. Refresh becomes a slow background raster sweep, as on a Williams tube.
why: Removes the access transistor and its leakage tail (fact 3); a floating island leaks only through dielectric, so retention could reach hours and refresh energy drop >100x; periphery shrinks to beam drivers (fact 7). Open risk: 10-100 ns spot access with fast deflection.

title: Twistor-inspired spiral-ribbon channel for a long, compact access transistor
idea: Borrow Bell Labs' twistor, a helical magnetic tape wound on a wire: grow the access-transistor channel as a helical silicon or oxide-semiconductor ribbon spiralling up a dielectric core inside a 4F2 pillar, with the wordline filling the spiral gap as the gate. Two to three turns give an effective channel length 5-8x the pillar height with no extra footprint.
why: A long channel flattens DIBL and short-channel Vt roll-off, which feed the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3); ~10x lower median leakage and a tighter tail could stretch refresh 4-8x at equal density.

title: Static induction transistor revival as an oxide-free access switch
idea: Revive Nishizawa's 1950s static induction transistor: a vertical pillar whose current is pinched off by buried p+ junction gates, with no gate dielectric and no gate-drain overlap, so the off state is a pure electrostatic potential barrier. With no MOS overlap there is no gate-induced drain leakage and no oxide-trap-assisted tunnelling, the two mechanisms behind the DRAM tail.
why: Attacks the GIDL and trap-assisted tail (fact 3), with a claimed 10x tail reduction; junction gates swing ~1-1.5 V instead of a ~3 V wordline, so wordline CV2 drops 2-4x (fact 10).

title: Kelvin curb-sending write pulses that cancel high-k dielectric soakage
idea: Revive Lord Kelvin's 1860s 'curb sender' for the transatlantic cable and the analog designers' dielectric-absorption compensation: each write or restore pulse gets a calibrated overshoot followed by a short reverse curb, pre-charging the slow Curie-von Schweidler polarization of the ZrO2/HfO2 storage capacitor. The apparent charge loss in the first milliseconds after a write, which today eats retention margin, goes away.
why: High-k relaxation removes a few percent of signal after each write and shows up as lost retention margin (facts 1, 3); recovering 5-10% of signal could stretch the refresh interval ~1.5-2x with only driver-timing changes.

title: Parametron-pumped refresh: global 2f pump restores charge without sensing
idea: Revive Goto's 1954 parametron, in which a pump at twice the signal frequency amplifies whichever phase is already present: give each cell a tiny MOS varactor coupled to its storage node and drive a global plate-line pump, so stored charge is parametrically amplified toward its own rail and bits are restored in place without row activation or sense amps.
why: Refresh costs ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3); in-place parametric restoration would make refresh bandwidth-free and cut its energy several-fold, because no bitlines swing.

title: Plasma-panel sustain refresh: threshold-gated global top-up pulses
idea: Revive the AC plasma display's inherent memory, in which a global sustain waveform re-fires only the cells that already hold wall charge: place a sharp threshold element (for example a punch-through diode) between each storage node and a shared sustain plane, then pulse the plane. Only nodes still above threshold (stored 1s) conduct and are topped up to full, while 0s stay below threshold and are left alone.
why: Makes refresh an unaddressed broadcast with no sense amps (facts 3, 8): no row activations, no 128x overfetch, and no row-hammer exposure from refresh (fact 9). Refresh energy could fall 5-10x and its bandwidth cost to ~0.

title: Selectron flood-holding: global photocurrent keeps nodes bistable, no refresh
idea: Revive RCA's 1948 Selectron and the Tektronix bistable storage tube, in which a continuous electron flood held each element at one of two stable potentials: a weak backside IR flood lets each storage node's photodiode supply a tiny current that balances leakage. A per-node negative-differential-resistance element gives the node two stable points (0 and VDD), so cells self-latch at picowatt levels instead of decaying.
why: Removes refresh as an operation (fact 3); standby power becomes flood power, targeted at under 1/10 of refresh power for 32-64 Gb dies.

title: Acoustic charge transport conveyor for refresh, revived from delay lines
idea: Revive mercury and magnetostrictive delay-line memory, together with 1980s acoustic charge transport: a surface acoustic wave launched across a piezoelectric overlayer carries charge packets from storage wells down a column to one regenerating amplifier and back. Refresh becomes continuous recirculation through one amplifier per column instead of row activations.
why: Refresh energy concentrates in one optimized regenerator per column, and transport is driven by a single transducer (fact 3); targets 3-5x lower refresh energy, with refresh fully hidden from the command bus.

title: Z80 R-register reborn: inference weight sweeps certified as refresh
idea: Revive the Zilog Z80's trick of refreshing DRAM during opcode fetch: the memory controller tracks which rows were read within the retention window and suppresses explicit refresh for them. LLM inference streams every weight row once per token (~20-50 ms), so the scheduler orders weight reads to touch every row within tREFW and weight regions in HBM become self-refreshing.
why: Removes most explicit refresh for weight-resident HBM (facts 3, 5); weights often fill 50-80% of capacity, so refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax fall roughly in proportion.

title: CRT flyback energy recovery for raster-like refresh sweeps
idea: Revive the television horizontal-deflection flyback circuit, which recycled deflection energy through an LC resonance on every scan line: refresh sweeps rows on a fixed periodic raster, so an on-package resonant LC tank drives the 3 V refresh wordlines and bitline precharge. Most of the CV2 energy returns to the tank at each refresh step instead of being dissipated.
why: Attacks the stuck CV2 energy (fact 10) and refresh's ~46 fJ/bit (fact 3), with 50-70% recovery of wordline and bitline swing energy during refresh.

title: Crested-barrier MIM tunnel diode as a two-terminal access device
idea: Revive Mead's 1960 metal-insulator-metal tunnel-emitter work and Likharev's crested-barrier proposal: a nitride/alumina/nitride trilayer with a peaked barrier gives Fowler-Nordheim nonlinearity steep enough that current at half bias is ~1e-9 of full-bias current. It serves as a two-terminal access device between capacitor and bitline, selected by plate-line pulsing, so access devices can stack in BEOL above logic.
why: Removes the silicon access transistor and its leakage tail (fact 3), and enables multi-tier BEOL stacking without lateral transistors (fact 2).

title: Magnetostrictive-squeezed Mott switch from delay-line wire technology
idea: Revive the magnetostrictive nickel-wire delay line: wordline current through a Galfenol (Fe-Ga) strip strains an adjacent nanoscale piezoresistive Mott material (SmSe-class) into its metallic phase, opening the cell. With no current the material relaxes to its insulating phase, ~1e5x more resistive, and there is no semiconductor junction to leak.
why: Isolation comes from a band-gapped insulator at zero strain rather than a subthreshold MOSFET (fact 3); galvanic separation between wordline and channel also removes wordline-coupling row-hammer paths (fact 9).

title: Purdue GaAs heterojunction storage well revived on silicon
idea: Revive the 1980s-90s Purdue AlGaAs/GaAs DRAM cells, which held charge for hours at room temperature because electrons sat in a well bounded by a wide-gap barrier: integrate a selectively grown heterostructure storage well (AlGaAs/GaAs, or GaP/AlP, which is lattice-closer to Si) on silicon, so stored charge can escape only by thermionic emission over 0.4-1 eV band offsets.
why: Storage-node leakage is set by the band offset rather than by junction or trap generation (fact 3); retention orders of magnitude longer would make refresh rare.

title: Vacuum-tube getter revived inside sealed BEOL cavities
idea: Revive the barium flash getter that kept vacuum tubes clean for decades: deposit a non-evaporable Zr-V-Fe getter film in a sealed cavity over each array mat, activated by the final anneal. It keeps absorbing the hydrogen and moisture that would otherwise migrate to access-transistor interfaces over life, creating trap-assisted leakage and variable retention time.
why: Keeps the tail stable (fact 3) over a 10-year life, so the ~2x refresh guardband can shrink; targets a 1.5-2x longer refresh interval and fewer VRT failures.

title: Keithley driven-guard cell: a follower nulls access-transistor Vds
idea: Revive the electrometer's driven guard, which kills leakage by holding a node's surroundings at the node's own voltage: split the access path into two series transistors with a tiny cell-local node between them. A zero-Vt native source follower from the storage node drives that local node, so the inner transistor sees Vds near 0 in hold and its subthreshold leakage falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Directly attacks the subthreshold part of the tail (fact 3): 10-100x longer retention for 1.5-2x cell area, which is worth it in a refresh-free tier.

title: Core-memory thermistor compensation: servo the off-wordline to leakage minimum
idea: Revive core memory's thermistor-compensated drive currents: a replica access transistor in each bank continuously measures total off-leakage (subthreshold plus GIDL), and a small dither loop holds the negative wordline voltage at the leakage minimum, which shifts with temperature and aging.
why: Fixed negative-wordline levels are set for the worst case and leave 3-10x leakage on the table across temperature (fact 3); tracking the minimum could double refresh intervals at hot corners.

title: Armstrong superregenerative sensing to read deeply decayed cells
idea: Revive Armstrong's 1922 superregenerative receiver: replace the single latch with a quenched regenerative sense stage whose exponential build-up time encodes the initial bitline differential, read by a time-to-digital comparator. It resolves signals 5-10x smaller than today's ~100 mV margin.
why: If sensing works at 10-20% of nominal charge, cells can decay far longer before refresh (fact 3) and a smaller Cs becomes usable (fact 1), giving 3-5x longer refresh intervals.

title: Coincident-current selection: AND-gated access for column-selective refresh
idea: Revive core memory's coincident-current selection: each cell's access path has two series gates, one on the row wordline and one on a column-select line, so only the cell at the intersection opens. Refresh can then target only the few weak columns flagged at test, and reads stop overfetching whole pages.
why: Refresh energy scales with the number of weak cells rather than whole rows (fact 3), and the 128x overfetch disappears (fact 8): about 1.3x cell area for potentially 10x lower refresh energy.

title: Atlas one-level store: lifetime-tagged pages that never get refreshed
idea: Revive the 1962 Manchester Atlas one-level store, whose hardware page tables tracked residency: add a lifetime-class bit to page-table entries and to the memory controller. Tensors rewritten faster than the retention time (activations, gradient buffers, ring buffers) go into rows marked no-refresh, and the OS guarantees each is rewritten within the certified retention time.
why: Short-lived AI data can be a large share of training memory; skipping refresh for it cuts refresh energy and the bandwidth tax roughly in proportion (fact 3), with no device change.

title: Sperry MNOS shadow trap: access transistor stores a sleep copy
idea: Revive Sperry's 1967 metal-nitride-oxide-semiconductor memory: give the access transistor a thin nitride charge-trap layer. On entering deep sleep, a row-by-row pulse injects trap charge according to each cell's bit (1e5-1e6 cycles is ample for sleep events) and the array powers off with zero refresh; on wake, the trap-shifted Vt is sensed and rewritten to the capacitor.
why: Removes self-refresh power, 16-33% of idle (fact 3), for idle servers and phones: zero retention power during sleep.

title: Plated-wire revival: coated bitline wires with strap-defined junctionless access
idea: Revive Univac's plated-wire memory, in which crossing word straps addressed a continuous film on a wire: coat vertical bitline wires conformally (ALD) with a thin junctionless semiconductor shell. Each horizontal wordline strap wraps the wire and gates, all around, a shell segment linking the wire to an adjacent ring capacitor, so transistors are defined by strap crossings rather than per-cell lithography or doping.
why: No implanted junctions means no junction leakage and no GIDL hot spots (fact 3); strap-defined devices suit multi-tier 3D (fact 2) and need fewer EUV layers (fact 4).

title: Cryosar freeze-out barrier access device for cryogenic memory tiers
idea: Revive IBM's 1959 cryosar, which switched by impact ionization of frozen-out impurities: at 40-77 K, a lightly doped silicon region between storage node and bitline insulates because its dopants are frozen out. A wordline field pulse impact-ionizes the donors so the region conducts for nanoseconds, then it refreezes.
why: Off-state leakage is limited by frozen-out carriers and is effectively zero (fact 3); for memory co-located with cryogenic AI or quantum hardware, refresh disappears and the cell needs no MOS gate stack.

title: Grid-leak self-biased wordlines replace the negative wordline pump
idea: Revive vacuum-tube grid-leak bias, in which a capacitor and leak resistor made a negative grid bias from the signal itself: each local wordline driver ends every activation by coupling its falling edge through a small MIM capacitor to undershoot below ground. The negative off-level relaxes slowly through a high-resistance leak, so recently used rows (hammer aggressors and their neighbors) sit deepest off.
why: Removes or shrinks the negative-wordline charge pump and its distribution in the periphery (fact 7), and deepens off-bias exactly where leakage and disturbance are worst (facts 3, 9).

title: Purdue SiC DRAM revival on U.S. SiC wafers for refresh-free tiers
idea: Revive the 1990s Purdue 6H/4H-SiC DRAM cells, which retained charge for hours at room temperature: build 4H-SiC access transistors and storage capacitors on 200 mm SiC wafers grown in North Carolina and processed in New York SiC fabs, accepting ~90 nm-class geometry for a retention tier that almost never refreshes.
why: SiC's 3.3 eV bandgap cuts intrinsic generation leakage by >1e10 versus Si (fact 3), so refresh energy is ~0; the supply chain is all U.S. and needs no EUV (fact 4). Density is lower, so it targets idle or standby capacity.

title: Neutron transmutation doping at U.S. research reactors for implant-free channels
idea: Revive 1970s neutron transmutation doping, used for power-device silicon: irradiate silicon at U.S. research reactors (for example the University of Missouri reactor) so Si-30 transmutes into uniformly distributed phosphorus. Access-transistor wells then form without implantation, removing the implant-damage clusters that seed trap-assisted leakage.
why: The extreme tail cells come largely from implant-damage defects (fact 3); implant-free, uniform wells could cut tail cells per die several-fold and allow longer refresh.

title: Crucible-free float-zone wafers: long carrier lifetime, no quartz crucibles
idea: Revive float-zone crystal growth, sidelined for CMOS by Czochralski: grow nitrogen-doped 200-300 mm FZ silicon in U.S. plants, so storage-node junctions sit in oxygen-free, long-lifetime silicon where generation leakage (proportional to 1/lifetime) is lower. No high-purity quartz crucible is consumed.
why: Lowers storage-node junction generation leakage 2-5x (fact 3) and removes the Spruce Pine HPQ crucible chokepoint (resources).

title: Spindt molybdenum-cone vacuum access switch with zero channel leakage
idea: Revive SRI's 1968 Spindt molybdenum-cone field emitters and the vacuum triode: each cell's access device is a nanoscale vacuum gap with a tip made of Colorado-mined molybdenum and a gate ring. In the off state the vacuum holds no carriers, so leakage is only Fowler-Nordheim tunnelling, negligible at hold fields; build on 130-90 nm U.S. lines with wafer-level vacuum sealing.
why: Eliminates the leakage tail at the physics level (fact 3); molybdenum replaces China-sourced tungsten (resources), and no EUV is needed (fact 4).

title: Western Electric relay contacts reborn as NEM access relays
idea: Revive the Bell System's palladium-contact telephone relays: each access device is a nanoelectromechanical relay with palladium/platinum contacts from Montana's Stillwater mines, built with the aluminum-hinge micromirror MEMS process already run at high volume in Texas, which shows >1e12 switching cycles. An open contact leaks nothing.
why: Zero off-state leakage (fact 3) so refresh vanishes, and galvanic isolation blocks row-hammer coupling (fact 9); built in U.S. MEMS fabs without EUV. Endurance toward 1e15 cycles is the main risk.

title: Moll-Tarui ferroelectric transistor as a sleep-only Vt shifter
idea: Revive the 1963 Moll-Tarui ferroelectric-gate transistor, but switch it only when entering and leaving long idle: a thin HZO layer, using hafnium refined in Albany, Oregon, sits in the access-transistor gate stack. It is poled to raise Vt ~0.4-0.5 V during self-refresh and re-poled to low Vt on wake, so endurance needs are only ~1e6-1e8 events.
why: A ~0.45 V Vt shift at ~80 mV/decade cuts subthreshold leakage by ~5 decades, so self-refresh intervals can grow 100x or more (then limited by junction and GIDL leakage), cutting the 16-33% idle-power share (fact 3).

title: AMI VMOS revival: crystal-etched V-groove access transistors
idea: Revive 1970s VMOS, which American Microsystems used for memories: KOH anisotropic etching produces self-limiting {111} V-grooves whose geometry is set by the crystal, and epitaxial or diffusion depth sets the channel length. A uniform vertical access transistor forms with a U.S.-built 1X stepper and no EUV.
why: Crystal-defined geometry removes the CD variation that widens the Vt and leakage tail (fact 3), and avoids the single EUV supplier (fact 4).

title: Silicon-on-sapphire storage nodes on U.S.-grown sapphire
idea: Revive Autonetics' 1963 silicon-on-sapphire, updated with solid-phase regrowth and laser anneal: build the array on sapphire wafers grown in New Hampshire and Illinois, so storage-node diffusions have no junction to a substrate. The insulating substrate also removes substrate-coupled noise and soft-error charge collection.
why: Removes the storage-node-to-substrate junction leakage component (fact 3) and soft errors with U.S. supply: 2-5x longer retention if the regrown silicon quality holds.

title: ETA-10 liquid-nitrogen memory tier using U.S. air separation
idea: Revive ETA Systems' 1987 ETA-10 supercomputer, which ran CMOS boards immersed in liquid nitrogen: put DRAM and HBM modules in LN2 baths made on site by U.S. air-separation units. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by >1e6, so refresh intervals stretch from 64 ms to minutes, and lower Vt allows lower wordline voltage.
why: Nearly eliminates refresh (fact 3), and lower voltages cut CV2 (fact 10); nitrogen comes from air, so the cooling needs no helium and has no Qatar exposure.

title: Bell Labs CCD memory revived: charge rings with one regenerator
idea: Revive the 1970s CCD serial memories (invented at Bell Labs in 1969, later sold as CCD RAMs): store bits as charge packets in gated MOS potential wells with no per-bit contact or junction, arranged in short rings that pass one regeneration amplifier. Build them at relaxed nodes on U.S. CCD and imager fab processes.
why: There is no per-bit access transistor or junction leakage path (fact 3), refresh happens naturally as charge circulates, and few contacts means lighter lithography (fact 4). Latency of ~100 ns to 1 us makes it a capacity tier.

title: Bell Labs electret back-gate holds access devices deeply off
idea: Revive Sessler and West's 1962 Bell Labs foil electret: implant a permanent negative trapped-charge layer, charged by corona or electron beam, into the Al2O3/SiO2 buried oxide under thin-body access transistors. This gives a built-in ~1 V reverse back bias with no charge pump, on U.S. FD-SOI lines; a boosted front-gate pulse restores on-current.
why: Raises hold Vt with no bias-generation power or periphery (facts 3, 7), cutting subthreshold leakage 10-100x.

title: IBM X-ray proximity lithography revived for uniform access pillars
idea: Revive IBM's 1990s X-ray lithography program in Vermont with a U.S.-built compact inverse-Compton light source: ~1 nm X-rays expose access-transistor pillars with near-vertical, highly uniform sidewalls and negligible diffraction-driven CD variation, replacing EUV for the critical access layers.
why: Pillar CD variation drives Vt variation and the leakage tail (fact 3); ~2x tighter CD sigma shortens the tail, and the single-supplier EUV dependence goes away (fact 4).

title: ESI laser trimming revived to heal weak access transistors
idea: Revive 1970s Portland-made laser trimming of resistors: after a retention test, a U.S.-built infrared picosecond laser fires through backside-thinned silicon to anneal the gate region of the ppm-level worst-leakage cells, healing trap clusters and raising each die's retention floor.
why: The refresh interval is set by the worst few cells (fact 3); repairing the bottom 1e-6 of the tail could stretch tREFW 2-4x.

title: 1968 zinc-oxide TFT revived as indium- and gallium-free access device
idea: Revive Boesen and Jacobs' 1968 ZnO thin-film transistor with modern ALD: an amorphized nitrogen/Mg-alloyed ZnO channel, using zinc from Alaska and Tennessee, forms BEOL access transistors with ultralow off-current from its 3.3 eV gap. It avoids IGZO's indium and gallium, both refined mostly abroad.
why: Oxide-semiconductor-level leakage gives multi-second retention (fact 3), with an all-U.S. element supply and BEOL stacking (fact 2).

title: Five-star tube grading reborn: retention-graded DRAM for relaxed refresh
idea: Revive the military practice of hand-selecting premium 'five-star' vacuum tubes: test every U.S.-made DRAM die for retention on U.S. testers, bin the tail-free fraction as long-retention parts certified for a 4-8x refresh interval, and sell them at a premium to U.S. hyperscalers whose controllers apply the certified interval.
why: Monetizes the natural retention distribution (fact 3): 4-8x less refresh energy and bandwidth on graded parts with no process change, and a business case for domestic fabs.

title: Manhattan Project parallel paths for a refresh-free access device
idea: Revive the Manhattan Project's parallel uranium-enrichment strategy: fund four competing access-device routes (SiC, vacuum nano-gap, NEM relay, zinc oxide) at four U.S. sites against one fixed spec (>=10 s retention at 85 C, <=30 ns access, >=1e16 cycles), with shared test vehicles and a hard down-select at 18 months.
why: De-risks the physics of fact 3 in parallel and shortens time to a solution, concentrating domestic capital on the access device, the biggest refresh lever.

title: Molybdenum-gate MOS revived: graded-work-function wordlines that cut GIDL
idea: Revive the refractory molybdenum-gate MOSFETs of the 1970s: replace tungsten buried wordlines with Colorado-mined molybdenum whose nitrogen content is graded with depth, so the gate work function is high over the channel (good Vt) and low where the gate overlaps the drain (less band bending), suppressing GIDL.
why: GIDL is a dominant tail mechanism (fact 3), targeted at ~10x lower; also removes dependence on China's ~80% share of tungsten.

title: Xerographic amorphous-selenium photoconductor as optically gated access switch
idea: Revive xerography's amorphous-selenium photoreceptor (dark resistivity ~1e14-1e15 ohm-cm) and the vidicon target: each cell's access element is a tiny a-Se photoconductor between bitline and capacitor, gated by light from silicon-nitride waveguide wordlines. Selenium is refined in Utah and the waveguides come from U.S. photonics foundries.
why: Dark off-state leakage sits far below MOS subthreshold (fact 3), and optical wordlines remove wordline-to-cell electrical coupling (fact 9) and the 3 V wordline swing (fact 10). Photoconductor response time limits speed.

title: Domestic heavy water revived for deuterium-passivated access transistors
idea: Revive the U.S. heavy-water production of the 1950s to supply domestic deuterium for high-pressure D2 anneals of access transistors and buried-wordline interfaces. Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and wordline-stress depassivation far better than Si-H, so the interface traps behind GIDL and variable retention stay passivated over life.
why: Stabilizes the leakage tail and VRT (fact 3), letting refresh guardbands shrink 1.5-2x, with a secure domestic D2 supply.

title: 1952 Bell licensing redux: open-license a low-leakage access cell
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1952 transistor licensing symposium, which sold patent rights cheaply to any firm and seeded an industry: a national lab or consortium develops a refresh-relaxed access-device module and licenses it, with a process design kit and test structures, to every U.S. fab for a nominal fee.
why: Multiplies domestic low-refresh memory capacity (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability) and cuts each fab's R&D bill and time to market.

title: 1 Mb-era fat cell revived at 65 nm, stacked by bonding
idea: Revive 1980s cells with 30+ fF capacitors and long-channel access transistors on existing U.S. 65-90 nm fabs to get second-scale retention, then recover density by hybrid-bonding 8-16 thinned dies into one stack, using a direct-bond process invented in North Carolina.
why: Trades area for retention, so refresh is ~0 (fact 3); avoids EUV entirely (fact 4), and running on depreciated U.S. fabs cuts capital intensity.

title: Energy Star for memory: label DIMMs by idle refresh watts
idea: Revive the EPA's 1992 Energy Star program, which pushed PCs into sleep modes: create an Energy Star memory tier based on measured self-refresh watts per GB at 45 C, and require the top tier in federal procurement, rewarding low-leakage access devices from U.S. fabs.
why: Creates market pull for cutting refresh energy (fact 3), which is 16-33% of idle memory power, and steers U.S. data-center buying.

title: GE's SCR revived as thyristor RAM cells on U.S. thin-SOI
idea: Revive GE's 1957 silicon-controlled rectifier and the thin-silicon thyristor RAM abandoned around 2012: a gate-coupled pnpn thyristor in thin silicon latches on at a picoamp holding current to store a 1 and stays blocked for a 0, switched by a gate-coupled pulse. Build it on an existing U.S. FD-SOI line.
why: The bistable latch removes refresh (fact 3) and needs no capacitor (fact 1), at near-1T density on a U.S. fab with no EUV; the trade is ~pA-per-bit holding power instead of refresh power.
